::: {.lead}
The shuttle of *Star Dock* finally gets its controls. The first test is a
disaster: on a fast laptop the shuttle races, on an old one it crawls; it
flies faster diagonally; it always points to the right, even when it flies
up; it stops dead when the key is released; it flies through the hangar
walls; and the sprite is drawn in the wrong place. Each problem has a
mathematical fix that you already know: vectors (lectures 2–6), angles
(lectures 7–8) and transformations (lectures 9–14). In this case study you
build the movement of one 2D object, step by step, and solve one part of it
together with a team. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary game-loop delta-time frame-rate-independence input-vector unit-vector velocity atan2 acceleration damping surface-normal reflection-vector bounciness trs-matrix team-roles >}}

## 27.1 Motion per frame with Δt

The game loop moves the shuttle a little in every frame. The size of that
step must depend on the time of the frame (@fig-steps).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.1 — Motion per frame"}
Each frame takes $\Delta t$ seconds (1/60 s at 60 fps). With velocity
$\vec{v}$ (units per second):
$$\vec{p}_{\text{new}} = \vec{p} + \vec{v} \cdot \Delta t.$$
This is **frame-rate independence**: at 30, 60 or 144 fps the shuttle
covers the same distance per second.
:::

![The same second at 30 and at 60 fps.](images/frame-steps.png){#fig-steps width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.1 — 30 or 60 fps"}
Speed 5 units per second, to the right.

1. At 60 fps: each step is $5 \cdot \frac{1}{60} \approx 0.083$; 60 steps give
   5 units.
2. At 30 fps: each step is $5 \cdot \frac{1}{30} \approx 0.167$; 30 steps give
   5 units.
3. Without $\Delta t$ ("move 0.083 every frame"), the 30 fps laptop moves
   only 2.5 units per second.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
void Update() {
    transform.position += (Vector3)(velocity * Time.deltaTime);
}
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using a fixed step per frame. The game then runs faster on fast computers
and slower on slow ones.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Δt"}
A meteor flies at 12 units per second. Compute its step per frame at 30,
60 and 144 fps, and check that each gives 12 units per second.

*Your result:* three steps and three checks.
:::

## 27.2 Input and diagonal movement

Keys or a stick give an **input vector** (@fig-diag).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.2 — Normalized input"}
Right gives (1, 0), up gives (0, 1); right + up gives (1, 1) with length
$\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$. To fly at the same speed in every direction,
**normalize** the input when its length is greater than 1:
$$\vec{d} = \frac{\text{input}}{|\text{input}|}, \qquad \vec{v} = \text{speed} \cdot \vec{d}.$$
A stick can give a length below 1 (half pushed): keep it, for slow
movement.
:::

![Diagonal input.](images/diagonal.png){#fig-diag width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.2 — The fast diagonal"}
1. Speed 5, input (1, 1): $\vec{v} = (5, 5)$, $|\vec{v}| = 5\sqrt{2} \approx
   7.07$: 41 % too fast.
2. Normalized: $(1, 1)/1.41 \approx (0.71, 0.71)$; $\vec{v} \approx (3.54,
   3.54)$; $|\vec{v}| = 5$.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/move-lab.html" poster="sims/move-lab.png" title="Move Lab: fly the shuttle of Star Dock" height="820" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Normalizing (0, 0). A zero vector has no direction: dividing by its length
0 gives an error. Check the length first.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Diagonals"}
1. In **Move Lab**, fly ↗ with "normalize input" off and on. Write both
   speeds.
2. Compute the velocity for input (−1, 1) and speed 8, normalized.

*Your result:* two speeds and one vector.
:::

## 27.3 Facing the velocity

The shuttle should point where it flies (@fig-face).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.3 — Facing with atan2"}
If the sprite is drawn facing $+x$, its rotation angle is
$$\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(v_y, v_x).$$
Turn only when the speed is not 0; otherwise keep the last angle.
:::

![Turn the ship to face its velocity.](images/facing.png){#fig-face width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.3 — Three directions"}
1. $\vec{v} = (3, 4)$: $\operatorname{atan2}(4, 3) \approx 53.1°$.
2. $\vec{v} = (0, 5)$: 90°. $\vec{v} = (-5, 0)$: 180°.
3. $\vec{v} = (-3, -4)$: $\operatorname{atan2}(-4, -3) \approx -126.9°$
   (the same as 233.1°).
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
if (velocity.sqrMagnitude > 0.0001f) {
    float deg = Mathf.Atan2(velocity.y, velocity.x) * Mathf.Rad2Deg;
    transform.rotation = Quaternion.Euler(0, 0, deg);
}
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing atan2(x, y) instead of atan2(y, x): the angle is then measured from
the y-axis, and the ship points the wrong way.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Facing"}
Compute the facing angle for $\vec{v} = (5, 5)$, $(-4, 3)$ and $(0, -2)$.

*Your result:* three angles.
:::

## 27.4 Acceleration and damping

Real ships do not start and stop at once (@fig-accel).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.4 — Acceleration and damping"}
- **Acceleration** $\vec{a}$ changes the velocity: $\vec{v} \mathrel{+}=
  \vec{a} \cdot \Delta t$, up to a maximum speed.
- **Damping** slows it down when no key is pressed: $\vec{v} \mathrel{\times}=
  (1 - k \cdot \Delta t)$ in each frame, with a damping factor $k$.
:::

![Speed over time.](images/accel.png){#fig-accel width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.4 — Speeding up and slowing down"}
1. $a = 10$, max speed 5: the shuttle reaches 5 after $5/10 = 0.5$ s.
2. Released, with $k = 4$ at 60 fps: each frame multiplies the speed by
   $1 - 4/60 \approx 0.933$: $5 \to 4.67 \to 4.36 \to \ldots$
3. After one second (60 frames): $5 \cdot 0.933^{60} \approx 0.08$: almost
   stopped.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Damping without $\Delta t$ (×0.9 every frame): the ship stops faster on
fast computers. Use $1 - k \cdot \Delta t$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Smooth flight"}
In **Move Lab**, switch on "accelerate" and "face the velocity". Fly, then
let go. Compute: with $a = 8$ and max speed 6, when is the max speed
reached?

*Your result:* a description and a time.
:::

## 27.5 Bouncing off walls

When the shuttle hits a hangar wall, its velocity is reflected
(@fig-bounce).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.5 — Reflected velocity"}
With the unit normal $\vec{n}$ of the wall (pointing into the hangar):
$$\vec{v}\,' = \vec{v} - 2(\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n})\,\vec{n}.$$
The part of $\vec{v}$ along the wall stays; the part into the wall turns
around. With **bounciness** $e$ (0 to 1): $\vec{v}\,' = \vec{v} - (1 + e)(\vec{v}
\cdot \vec{n})\,\vec{n}$.
:::

![A bounce.](images/bounce.png){#fig-bounce width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.5 — Floor and wall"}
1. Floor, $\vec{n} = (0, 1)$, $\vec{v} = (4, -3)$: $\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n} = -3$;
   $\vec{v}\,' = (4, -3) - 2(-3)(0, 1) = (4, 3)$.
2. With $e = 0.8$: $\vec{v}\,' = (4, -3) - 1.8(-3)(0, 1) = (4, 2.4)$.
3. Right wall, $\vec{n} = (-1, 0)$, $\vec{v} = (4, 3)$: $\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n} =
   -4$; $\vec{v}\,' = (4, 3) - 2(-4)(-1, 0) = (-4, 3)$.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/bounce-lab.html" poster="sims/bounce-lab.png" title="Bounce Lab: reflect the velocity" height="680" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Turning both parts: $(4, -3) \to (-4, 3)$. Only the part along the normal
changes its sign.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Bounces"}
1. In **Bounce Lab**, check Example 27.5 with e = 1 and e = 0.8.
2. Compute the bounce of $\vec{v} = (-2, 5)$ on the ceiling, $\vec{n} = (0, -1)$.

*Your result:* the lab results and one vector.
:::

## 27.6 Drawing the sprite: local to world

The game knows the shuttle's position, angle and size; the sprite's corners
are stored in **local space**. A TRS transform puts them into the world
(@fig-trs).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.6 — The sprite's transform"}
For a corner $\vec{c}$ in local space: first **scale** (S), then
**rotate** (R) by the facing angle, then **translate** (T) to the
position:
$$\vec{c}_{\text{world}} = T \cdot R \cdot S \cdot \vec{c}$$
(lecture 13). In homogeneous coordinates this is one $3 \times 3$ matrix.
:::

![Local corners to world.](images/sprite-trs.png){#fig-trs width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.6 — The nose of the shuttle"}
Scale 2, angle 90°, position (5, 3).

1. Nose (1, 0) → S → (2, 0) → R(90°) → (0, 2) → T → **(5, 5)**.
2. Back (−0.5, 0.5) → (−1, 1) → (−1, −1) → **(4, 2)**.
3. Back (−0.5, −0.5) → (−1, −1) → (1, −1) → **(6, 2)**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Translating before rotating: the shuttle then circles around the origin
instead of turning on the spot.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · World corners"}
Compute the world corners of the shuttle with scale 1, angle 180° and
position (2, 4).

*Your result:* three points.
:::

## Team activity: the drone mission

::: {.callout-note title="Team activity · The drone mission (about 20 minutes)"}
**Mission.** A repair drone of *Star Dock* starts at (2, 1) with speed 5 and
the input ↗. After 2 seconds it hits the hangar ceiling ($\vec{n} = (0, -1)$,
$e = 0.8$). Its sprite has scale 1.5.

**Team roles** (teams of three):

1. **Movement:** the normalized velocity, the position after 2 s at 60 fps
   (ignore the ceiling until then), the step per frame.
2. **Facing and drawing:** the facing angle before the hit, and the world
   position of the nose (1, 0) at the start.
3. **Bounce:** the velocity after the ceiling, and the new facing angle.

Each member solves one part and **checks** the part of one other member.
Then the team presents its solution in two minutes: one slide or one page,
with every step.

**Individual alternative.** A student who works alone solves all three
parts in order, checks each part with **Move Lab** or **Bounce Lab**, and
hands in one page with the steps.
:::

## Case study: Pilot Check

Before the shuttle may fly, the test pilots check six numbers of its
movement code: the step at 30 fps, the speed of a diagonal without
normalizing, the facing angle of (3, 4), the time to reach the max speed,
the velocity after a bounce on the floor, and the world position of the
sprite's nose. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
checks. In the mini-game below you choose the right result for each one.

{{< sim file="sims/pilot-check.html" poster="sims/pilot-check.png" title="Pilot Check: six numbers of the movement code" kind="game" height="440" >}}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*, 2nd
ed. (2011), Chapters 2 and 5. Nystrom, *Game Programming Patterns* (2014),
the chapter "Game Loop" (free online).

## Exercises

1. Write the update rule for the position with Δt.
2. Speed 9, 30 fps: what is the step per frame?
3. Why is a game without Δt slower on a slow computer?
4. What is the length of the input (1, −1)? Normalize it.
5. Speed 6 and input (1, 1), normalized: what is the velocity?
6. Facing angle for $\vec{v} = (-1, 1)$?
7. Facing angle for $\vec{v} = (0, -3)$?
8. $a = 12$, max speed 6: when is the max speed reached?
9. Damping with $k = 6$ at 60 fps: by which factor does the speed shrink in
   one frame?
10. Reflect $\vec{v} = (3, -2)$ on the floor $\vec{n} = (0, 1)$.
11. Reflect $\vec{v} = (-5, 1)$ on the left wall $\vec{n} = (1, 0)$.
12. In exercise 10, what is $\vec{v}\,'$ with $e = 0.5$?
13. Scale 1, angle 90°, position (3, 3): where is the nose (1, 0)?
14. Why must the sprite be rotated before it is translated?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. $\vec{p} \mathrel{+}= \vec{v} \cdot \Delta t$.
2. $9 / 30 = 0.3$.
3. It moves the same step per frame, and a slow computer has fewer frames
   per second.
4. $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$; $(0.71, -0.71)$.
5. $6 \cdot (0.71, 0.71) \approx (4.24, 4.24)$.
6. 135°.
7. −90° (or 270°).
8. $6 / 12 = 0.5$ s.
9. $1 - 6/60 = 0.9$.
10. $(3, 2)$.
11. $(5, 1)$.
12. $(3, -2) - 1.5(-2)(0, 1) = (3, 1)$.
13. (1, 0) → (0, 1) → (3, 4).
14. Otherwise it rotates around the origin of the world and moves away.
:::
